title: One Index Over Both Filter Columns
description: Filtering on two columns with no matching index scans; a single composite index over both lets the engine seek straight to the rows. Why it matters: multi-column filters are everywhere in real applications, and a single well-designed composite index often replaces several narrower ones.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson introduces **composite indexes** — indexes built on more than one column at a time — and shows why combining two so-so filter columns into a single index can be far more powerful than indexing either one alone.

Why does this happen? On their own, neither `WarehouseId` (only 50 distinct values) nor `ProductId` (only 6,000 distinct values) narrows things down enough to be worth a dedicated index by itself — either one alone would still match thousands of rows out of 300,000. But *together*, `WarehouseId = 35 AND ProductId = 1235` pins down just a handful of rows. A composite index built on both columns together can represent that combination directly, sorted first by warehouse, then by product within each warehouse.

Think of a warehouse directory organized first by aisle number, then by shelf number within each aisle. Neither "aisle 12" alone nor "shelf 3" alone tells you much — lots of aisles have a shelf 3, and aisle 12 has many shelves. But "aisle 12, shelf 3" together pins down one specific spot, and if the directory is sorted that way (aisle first, then shelf), you can jump straight there. A composite index does exactly that for a two-column filter: it doesn't help either column individually as much as it helps the *combination*.

## Scenario
An inventory check looks up one product in one warehouse: `WHERE WarehouseId = 35 AND ProductId = 1235`. With no matching index, finding a handful of rows scans all 300,000.

## Why it's slow
There's no index on these columns, so it's a **Clustered Index Scan**. Neither column alone is very selective (50 warehouses, 6,000 products), but *together* they pin down just a few rows — so the ideal index covers **both**.

## What to look for
- A full scan for a query that targets one warehouse/product pair.
- Reads across the whole table to return a tiny result.

## The concept
When a query filters on several columns with `AND`, a single **composite index** over those columns lets SQL Server seek straight to the matching rows: `(WarehouseId, ProductId)`. It's far better than two separate single-column indexes (which the engine would have to combine) and far better than no index at all. INCLUDE `Qty` so the index also covers what you select.
hints: No index covers WarehouseId and ProductId together, so the whole table is scanned.
The two columns together are highly selective; one composite index over both lets the engine seek.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Inventory_Wh_Prod ON Inventory(WarehouseId, ProductId) INCLUDE (Qty);
